title: Pressure-cooker pork ribs
subtitle: Tender, pull-from-the-bone ribs in 30 minutes
excerpt: Pork ribs cooked under pressure until the meat pulls cleanly from the bone, then finished under the grill with a sticky glaze. A low-and-slow result without the hours.
sourceNotes: The two-stage method, pressure-cook to tenderise, then glaze under heat, follows the approach used in American barbecue home cooking when an outdoor smoker is unavailable. The method is documented across American pressure-cooker cookbooks from the 1990s onwards.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pressure-cook the ribs up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Glaze and grill just before serving.

content.text: Pressure-cooker pork ribs use a two-stage method. The pressure cooker tenderises the meat in about 30 minutes. A short spell under a hot grill then crisps the surface and sets a sticky glaze. The result is tender meat that pulls from the bone, produced in less time than three hours in the oven.

Baby back ribs or spare ribs both work; spare ribs are meatier and have more fat, which keeps them juicy under pressure. Ask the butcher to remove the membrane from the back of the rack, or do it yourself with a sharp knife, it comes away in one piece and, if left on, stays tough throughout cooking.
The glaze is built from storecupboard ingredients, no specific brand needed. Sticky, slightly sweet, slightly hot is the aim.

Rub the racks with smoked paprika and salt on all sides. Cut into sections of 3 to 4 ribs to fit the pressure cooker. Stand the sections upright in the pot or stack if needed. Pour in {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock and add the bruised garlic. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 30 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 10 minutes, then quick-release the rest.

While the ribs cook, mix together the ketchup, soy sauce, honey, smoked paprika, grated garlic, and chilli powder to make the glaze. Heat the grill to high. Transfer the cooked ribs to a foil-lined baking tray. Brush generously with the glaze on both sides. Grill for 4 to 5 minutes until the glaze is sticky and starting to char at the edges. Brush with a second coat and return under the grill for 2 more minutes.

rows.symptom: The meat does not pull away from the bone easily
rows.cause: The ribs needed more time at pressure.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 10 minutes. At 40 minutes, the meat should come off the bone.

rows.symptom: The glaze burns before it sets
rows.cause: The grill was too close to the element, or the glaze contained too much sugar.
rows.fix: Move the tray down a level in the oven. The grill should char the glaze at the edges without burning the surface.

rows.cause: The stock level was too low, or the meat was spare ribs that had little marbling.
rows.fix: Ensure at least 200 ml of liquid in the pot before sealing. Baby back ribs are leaner and more prone to drying than spare ribs.

content.text: Ribs are a weekend dish, sticky, hands-on, and satisfying in a way that is more relaxed than formal. The pressure cooker version brings them within reach on a weekday evening rather than reserving them for barbecue season. Serve with coleslaw and potato wedges, or simply with bread to mop up the glaze.
